kurals.tamil:
உள்ளக் களித்தலும் காண மகிழ்தலும்
கள்ளுக்கில் காமத்திற் குண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullak kaliththalum kaana makizhdhalum
kallukkil kaamaththir kundu.
kurals.meaning: To be elated merely by thinking, and to rejoice merely by seeing: wine cannot do this, but love can.
kurals.elementary: A treat only makes you happy once you eat it. But when you miss someone you love, just thinking of them makes you smile, and seeing them makes you jump for joy. The poet says love is stronger than any treat, because it works even before it arrives.
kurals.university: The chapter title puṇarcci vitumpal combines puṇarcci (union, coming together) and vitumpal (eager longing, impatient haste); it belongs to the kaṟpu (wedded love) section and follows kuṟippaṟivuṟuttal, describing the eagerness of husband and wife to be reunited, an eagerness strong enough to override the playful sulking (ūṭal) that convention expects. The couplet contrasts kaḷ (toddy, palm wine) with kāmam (love): uḷḷak kaḷittal is intoxication from mere thought (uḷḷal, to think) and kāṇa makiḻtal is joy from mere sight, and neither belongs to wine, which must actually be drunk. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss it as two states (nilai) that wine lacks but love possesses; Solomon Pappaiah adds that thought excites without overwhelming the senses while sight overwhelms them; Kalaignar sums it up as ‘wine gives pleasure only when drunk, love gives it at a thought or a glance.’ The comparison with wine recurs in kural 1288 of this chapter and echoes the earlier chapter on abstaining from toddy (kaḷḷuṇṇāmai, ch. 93). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the gopis of Vraja hear Krishna’s flute on the autumn night, they drop whatever they are doing, milking, cooking, serving their families, and hurry toward the sound, already overwhelmed before they have even reached him.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata presents the gopis as so absorbed in Krishna that the mere sound and thought of him carries them away.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s lover, the gopis are intoxicated by love at a hint of the beloved, before any meeting.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.29.4-8 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; shares the idea of love overpowering at a mere sign, but it is devotional love for God and lacks the Kural’s explicit contrast with wine.

christianity.quote_or_event: “How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices!”
christianity.explanation: The bridegroom of the Song declares the delight of his beloved’s love to surpass wine itself.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same comparison: love outdoes wine in the joy it gives.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a direct match on love being better than wine, though the Song does not add the Kural’s point about thought and sight.

islam.quote_or_event: “Hail to thee, then, O LOVE, sweet madness! Thou who healest all our infirmities!”
islam.explanation: In the prologue to his Masnavi, the Sufi poet Rumi praises love as a sweet madness that cures every ill.
islam.tie_back: The Kural calls love an intoxication greater than wine; Rumi likewise names love a ‘sweet madness’, a delight beyond reason.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, Prologue (tr. E.H. Whinfield)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Whinfield’s abridged translation); a fair thematic match on love as intoxicating madness, though Rumi’s love is mystical and Sufi poetry is not scripture.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth— For thy love is better than wine.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs opens with the beloved’s longing and her declaration that love surpasses wine.
judaism.tie_back: This is the closest scriptural twin to the Kural’s claim that love gives a joy wine cannot.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917 version); a near one-to-one comparison of love and wine, without the Kural’s thought-and-sight distinction.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From lust springs grief, from lust springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that passionate desire, however sweet, is the root of grief and fear.
buddhism.tie_back: Where the Kural celebrates love as a delight greater than wine, the Buddhist view treats such intoxication as a source of suffering, so the parallel is one of contrast.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a next-best match by contrast, since Buddhism warns against the very passion the Kural praises.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana warns that sensual pleasures are like a fruit that is delicious at first and poisonous afterwards.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ranks love above wine as a delight; Jain teaching treats both alike as sweet poisons, so the parallel is a sharp contrast.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a next-best match by contrast, since the Jain monastic text rejects the pleasures the Kural praises.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes Eros as the fairest of the deathless gods, who loosens the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsel of all gods and men.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Theogony, Eros is a primal power whose effect on the mind is overwhelming, like a drug.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise presents love as a force that intoxicates the mind more surely than wine.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Theogony 120-122 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a reasonable match on love overpowering the mind, though Hesiod does not compare it with wine or speak of thought and sight.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that the greatest blessings come through a divine madness, and that the madness of love is the best of these, sent by the gods for the lover’s happiness.
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedrus, Plato reverses the usual view that love’s intoxication is merely harmful and calls it a god-given madness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s praise of love as an elation that comes at a thought or a glance is close to Plato’s idea of love as a blessed madness.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 244a-245c (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known argument; a good match on love as a beneficial intoxication, though Plato’s purpose is philosophical rather than a lover’s confession.

kurals.tamil:
தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை வேண்டும் பனைத்துணையும்
காமம் நிறைய வரின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thinaiththunaiyum oodaamai vaendum panaiththunaiyum
kaamam niraiya varin.
kurals.meaning: When love comes in fullness, as tall as a palmyra tree, one should not sulk even as much as a millet grain.
kurals.elementary: If you have a mountain of love for someone, it makes no sense to stay grumpy with them over a crumb-sized thing. The poet compares the love to a tall palm tree and the grumpiness to a tiny seed.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two proverbial Tamil measures against each other: tiṉai (Italian millet, the smallest grain) and paṉai (the palmyra palm, the tallest tree), each with tuṇai (‘measure, extent’). When kāmam comes niṟaiya (‘in fullness’) to the measure of a palmyra, one should not engage in ūṭal (lovers’ feigned sulking) even to the measure of a millet seed. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as general advice, while Solomon Pappaiah applies it specifically to the wife and her husband; in the traditional reading the heroine says this when her companion suggests she show displeasure at her husband’s long absence. Ūṭal is otherwise a valued convention of akam poetry (the final chapters 130-133 are devoted to it), so the couplet’s point is that eagerness for reunion overrides it here. Pope’s translation (‘Distrust can find no place small as the millet grain’) renders ūṭal loosely as distrust. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna, coming to Radha after she has withdrawn in wounded pride, pleads with her to give up her anger, telling her that her displeasure torments him and asking her to let love win over pique.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s Radha nurses mana (proud sulking) against Krishna, and Krishna begs her to set it aside.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same: where love is great, even a little sulking has no place.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known canto; a good match on a lover asked to abandon pique for love, though the speaker is the lover pleading rather than the beloved resolving.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as patient and slow to take offence.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s advice not to sulk even a little when love is great is a lover’s version of love that ‘is not easily provoked’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a solid match on love that refuses offence, though Paul speaks of charity in general, not romantic love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes marriage as a bond of tranquillity, affection and mercy.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ideal of spouses whose love leaves no room for petty sulking fits this picture of affection and mercy between mates.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a general match on marital affection, without the Kural’s specific point about sulking.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hatred stirreth up strifes; but love covereth all transgressions.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that love passes over offences while hatred feeds quarrels.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, great love leaves no room for nursing a grievance.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a good match on love overriding grievance, though it is general wisdom rather than about lovers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that resentment is ended only by letting it go.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural asks the lover to drop even the smallest resentment; the Buddhist verse gives the general principle, though in a far graver register.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a loose next-best match, since the verse concerns hatred, not a lover’s mild sulking.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra lists anger as the destroyer of love (priti), pride as the destroyer of humility, deceit as the destroyer of friendship, and greed as the destroyer of everything.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching names anger (krodha), one of the four passions (kashayas), as the specific enemy of affection.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns against even a millet-grain of sulking because it cuts against great love; the Jain verse explains why: anger destroys love.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.38 (verse numbering varies by edition; paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse not checked against a live translation in this session; a partial match, since the Jain text treats anger as a passion to be destroyed, not a lovers’ quarrel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, the poor old couple who welcomed the disguised gods, had lived together in perfect accord since youth, and asked only that neither should outlive the other.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s tale portrays a marriage so united that no discord ever came between the pair.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They are the picture of the Kural’s ideal: love so full that no sulking finds room.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth (told by the Roman poet Ovid); a loose match on unbroken marital harmony, with no mention of sulking or reunion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch advises newly married couples to guard against small quarrels and petty grievances, since harmony (homonoia) between husband and wife is the foundation of their shared life.
philosophy.explanation: His Conjugal Precepts repeatedly counsel spouses to let minor offences go quickly.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s advice to sulk not even a millet-grain’s worth is the same counsel, given in a lover’s voice.
philosophy._accuracy_note: General paraphrase of the treatise’s advice rather than a single precept; a partial match, more practical than passionate.

kurals.tamil:
பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும் கொண்கனைக்
காணா தமையல கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Paenaadhu petpavae seyyinum konkanaik
kaanaa thamaiyala kan.
kurals.meaning: Even if my husband slights me and does only as he pleases, my eyes cannot rest without seeing him.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a friend ignores you, and you feel hurt, but you still keep looking out for them at the window. The wife in this poem feels the same: even when her husband seems careless, her eyes keep searching for him.
kurals.university: Pēṇātu means ‘without caring for (me)’, ‘neglecting’, and peṭpavē ceyyiṉum ‘even if he does only what he desires’; koṇkaṉ (‘husband, the one who took me’) is the object of kāṇātu (‘without seeing’), and amaiyala kaṇ ‘the eyes do not rest/settle’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘my eyes do not settle without seeing my lover’, Puliyur Kesikan ‘my eyes find no peace’, and Kalaignar ‘though he does not embrace me and does what pleases him, my eyes are not at peace without seeing him’. The couplet shows the heroine’s will to resent overruled by her eyes’ longing, a motif that links to chapter 118 (kaṇvitumpaḻital, the eyes’ eager suffering). Pope’s prose explanation (‘Though my eyes disregard me and do what is pleasing to my husband’) takes the eyes as the subject of the first clause, a construal not followed by the modern commentators cited here. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the ‘song to the bumblebee’, a gopi rebukes Krishna’s messenger, calling Krishna fickle and ungrateful for leaving them, yet confesses that the women of Vraja cannot stop speaking and thinking of him.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis feel slighted by Krishna’s departure to Mathura but are unable to turn their minds away from him.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the wife in the Kural, they are neglected by the beloved yet cannot rest without him.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.47 (Bhramara Gita) (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter; a strong thematic match on longing that persists despite neglect, in a devotional frame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The bride of the Song cannot rest at night for longing to find her absent beloved.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the lover’s restlessness ends only when the beloved is seen.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good match on restless seeking, though the Song does not mention neglect by the beloved.

islam.quote_or_event: “And women in the city said, ‘The wife of al-'Azeez is seeking to seduce her slave boy; he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the wife of al-Aziz consumed by love for Joseph even though he refuses her.
islam.tie_back: Her love persists despite being spurned, as the Kural’s wife longs for a husband who slights her, though the Qur’anic context is an unlawful passion it criticises.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); only a partial match on love unmoved by rejection, in a morally very different context from the Kural’s married love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And if I say: ‘I will not make mention of Him, nor speak any more in His name’, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I weary myself to hold it in, but cannot.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah, mistreated for his calling, resolves to give it up but finds the fire in his heart too strong to contain.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise cannot hold back her longing for one who has slighted her.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a structural match on a resolution overpowered by inner fire, but the subject is prophecy, not love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada names not seeing the beloved as a specific form of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes that cannot rest without seeing the husband are exactly this pain, though the Buddha’s remedy is detachment rather than reunion.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it names the same pain of not seeing the beloved, but prescribes the opposite remedy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana describes the eye’s attachment to what it sees as a craving that is never satisfied.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes that cannot rest without seeing the husband show the same restless craving of sight, though the Jain text diagnoses it as bondage.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial match on the eyes’ unsatisfied longing, framed as a danger rather than as love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo, spurned by Narcissus, still follows him and pines for him, wasting away until only her voice remains.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Echo keeps loving a youth who scorns her and cannot tear herself away from him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, Echo is slighted by the one she loves yet cannot rest away from him.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth (Ovid’s Roman telling); a good match on love outlasting neglect, though Echo’s love is unrequited and ends tragically.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristophanes, in Plato’s Symposium, tells how lovers are halves of a once-whole being; when they find each other they do not wish to be parted even for a moment, and cannot say what they want except to be together.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s myth explains love as an irresistible longing for one’s missing half.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s eyes that will not rest until they see the husband reflect that longing for the missing half.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 192b-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous speech; a reasonable match on the need to be with the beloved, without the Kural’s element of neglect.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன்மன் தோழி அதுமறந்து
கூடற்கண் சென்றதுஎன் னெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ootarkan sendraenman thoazhi adhumarandhu
koodarkan sendradhuen nenju.
kurals.meaning: My friend, I set out intending to sulk, but my heart forgot all that and went straight toward reunion.
kurals.elementary: Imagine planning to stay cross with a friend who came back late from a trip, but the moment you see them you forget and run to hug them. That is what happens to the wife in this poem: her plan to be cross melts away.
kurals.university: The heroine addresses her companion (tōḻi): ūṭaṟkaṇ ceṉṟēṉ maṉ, ‘I did go toward sulking’, where the particle maṉ marks a past intention that came to nothing; but atu maṟantu, ‘forgetting it’, eṉ neñcu (‘my heart’) went kūṭaṟkaṇ, ‘toward union’. The neat opposition of ūṭal (lovers’ sulking) and kūṭal (coming together) carries the chapter’s theme: eagerness for reunion overruling the convention of feigned displeasure. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it this way; Solomon Pappaiah specifies that she planned to sulk over his fault before seeing him and forgot it once she saw him; Kalaignar generalises it as the special nature of love. The heart acting apart from the speaker’s will anticipates the next chapter, neñcoṭu pulattal (‘quarrelling with one’s heart’). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After nursing her anger through the night, Radha is persuaded by her friend that Krishna waits for her, and she goes to him, her pride dissolving as she enters the bower.
hinduism.explanation: In Jayadeva’s poem Radha’s resolve to stay offended gives way to her eagerness to meet Krishna.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine likewise sets out to sulk and finds her heart has gone to reunion instead.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the closing cantos; a good match on pique yielding to the desire for union, though in Jayadeva the change is coaxed by a friend.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes the experience of intending one thing and finding oneself doing another.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine intends to sulk but her heart carries her to embrace; the divided will is the same, though Paul speaks of moral struggle.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); only a structural match on will and action diverging, in a context of sin rather than love.

islam.quote_or_event: “Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that answering hostility with goodness can turn estrangement into close friendship.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows estrangement turning to closeness in a moment; the Qur’an names the same turn, though as a moral strategy rather than a lover’s impulse.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a loose match on enmity becoming closeness, without the Kural’s involuntary heart.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him; and they wept.”
judaism.explanation: Esau, who had set out with four hundred men against his brother, embraces Jacob the moment they meet.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, an intended hostility vanishes at the meeting and the heart runs to embrace.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a good structural match on grievance melting at sight, but between brothers rather than spouses.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada compares the mind to an arrow shaft that the wise must straighten, describing it as fickle, unsteady and hard to guard.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching recognises that the mind runs where it will unless it is trained.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart that forgets the plan and runs to reunion is an example of this unruly mind, though the Buddhist aim is to restrain it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse, not re-checked word for word in this session; a partial match on the mind outrunning intention, with the opposite evaluation.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, Gautama explains that the mind is an unruly, dreadful horse that runs about, and that he keeps it in check by the discipline of the Law.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana pictures the mind as a wild horse that bolts unless reined in.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart bolts toward reunion against the heroine’s plan; the Jain image captures that runaway mind, though it calls for restraint.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 23 (Kesi and Gautama) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known dialogue, cited without a verse number; a partial match on the mind running away, framed as something to master.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Procris flees in anger and shame over a test of fidelity, Cephalus seeks her out, and the two are reconciled and live for years in harmony.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s couple quarrel and part, but their love draws them back together.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, displeasure gives way to the stronger pull of reunion.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth (Ovid’s Roman telling); a partial match on reconciliation, though the quarrel is serious and the reunion not instantaneous.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, the charioteer of the soul tries to hold back the unruly horse, but at the sight of the beloved that horse drags the whole team forward toward him despite the charioteer’s resolve.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s image shows desire overpowering the reasoned intention of the soul when the beloved appears.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine intends to sulk, but her heart, like Plato’s horse, carries her straight to the beloved.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 253c-254e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous allegory; a strong match on desire overriding resolve at the beloved’s presence, though Plato goes on to praise restraint.

kurals.tamil:
எழுதுங்கால் கோல்காணாக் கண்ணேபோல் கொண்கன்
பழிகாணேன் கண்ட இடத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ezhudhungaal koalkaanaak kannaepoal konkan
pazhikaanaen kanda idaththu.
kurals.meaning: Just as the eye cannot see the brush that paints it with kohl, I cannot see my husband’s faults at the moment I see him.
kurals.elementary: Your eye can see everything around it, but it cannot see the little brush that touches it when someone puts on eyeliner, because it is too close. The wife says her husband’s faults are like that brush: when he is right in front of her, she cannot see them.
kurals.university: The simile draws on the practice of applying mai (collyrium, kohl) with a slender rod (kōl): eḻutuṅkāl, ‘while painting/applying’, the eye does not see the kōl, though it saw it a moment earlier. So too, kaṇṭa iṭattu (‘at the place/time of seeing him’), she does not see the paḻi (fault, blame) of her koṇkaṉ (husband). Solomon Pappaiah makes the comparison exact: the eye saw the rod before but not while it paints; she brooded on his fault in his absence but cannot see it in his presence. Kalaignar names the fault as his having left her. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan follow the same line. The domestic, almost tactile image is characteristic of the Kural’s Inbam section, and the couplet pairs closely with the next (1286). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Nala, who had abandoned Damayanti in the forest, is at last recognised and restored to her, she receives him without reproach, and the couple are reunited in joy.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata’s story of Nala and Damayanti ends with a wife whose grievance over desertion gives way entirely to reunion.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, Damayanti cannot hold her husband’s fault against him once he stands before her.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known story; a good match on a deserting husband’s fault forgotten at reunion, though the epic includes an exchange of explanations the Kural omits.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.”
christianity.explanation: Peter teaches that fervent love covers over many faults.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s wife experiences this directly: in her husband’s presence, love hides his faults from her sight.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good match on love covering faults, though Peter speaks of community love, not a wife’s perception.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘No blame will there be upon you today. Allah will forgive you; and He is the most merciful of the merciful.’”
islam.explanation: Joseph, meeting the brothers who wronged him, declares at once that he holds no blame against them.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the moment of meeting erases the fault that had been borne in absence.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a partial match on blame dissolving at meeting, but it is a brother’s forgiveness, not a lover’s blindness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that harpeth on a matter estrangeth a familiar friend.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that love chooses to cover an offence, while dwelling on it drives people apart.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife does not ‘harp on the matter’ once she sees her husband; love covers his fault.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a good match on love covering faults, though as deliberate wisdom rather than involuntary blindness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada observes that the faults of others are easily seen, while one’s own are hard to see, and that people winnow others’ faults like chaff.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching notes how perception of faults is distorted by one’s position and attachments.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows the reverse distortion: love so close that it cannot see the beloved’s fault, like the eye and the brush.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse, not re-checked word for word in this session; a loose match on biased fault-finding, inverted relative to the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the crane is produced from an egg, and the egg is produced from a crane, so they call desire the origin of delusion, and delusion the origin of desire.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that desire and delusion feed each other, clouding clear perception.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife cannot see her husband’s faults in his presence; in Jain terms her desire produces exactly this blindness (moha).
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial match explaining love’s blindness as delusion, which the Jain text condemns and the Kural treats tenderly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Troy fell, Menelaus went to kill his faithless wife Helen, but at the sight of her he threw down his sword and took her back.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the tradition recorded by Euripides and others, Helen’s presence alone undoes Menelaus’s resolve to punish her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise finds the fault she meant to punish invisible once she sees her husband.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested episode; a strong match on grievance vanishing at the sight of the beloved, though Helen’s fault was far graver.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates remarks that a lover finds every feature of his beloved charming: a snub nose he calls winsome, a hooked nose royal, a dark skin manly, a pale one divine, so that no blemish is ever seen.
philosophy.explanation: Plato observes that love transforms perception so that the beloved’s defects disappear or become virtues.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s insight exactly: in the beloved’s presence the lover cannot see faults.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic V, 474d-475a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a close match on love’s blindness to faults, though Plato uses it to illustrate a point about lovers of wisdom.

kurals.tamil:
காணுங்கால் காணேன் தவறாய காணாக்கால்
காணேன் தவறல் லவை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaanungaal kaanaen thavaraaya kaanaakkaal
kaanaen thavaral lavai.
kurals.meaning: When I see him, I see none of his faults; when I do not see him, I see nothing but his faults.
kurals.elementary: When your best friend is with you, you only remember how fun they are. When they are away and forgot to call, you can only think of what they did wrong. The wife in this poem notices she does exactly this with her husband.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a chiasmus of kāṇ- (‘see’): kāṇuṅkāl kāṇēṉ tavaṟāya (‘when I see [him], I do not see what is wrong’), kāṇākkāl kāṇēṉ tavaṟu allavai (‘when I do not see [him], I do not see what is not wrong’). The wordplay turns on two senses of seeing, physical sight of the husband and mental perception of faults. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second half as ‘I do not see the good things that are not faults’; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as ‘I see nothing but faults’. The couplet extends the previous one (1285) by adding the opposite case and so explains why the heroine plans to sulk in absence yet forgets it in presence (1284). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints the sandhi as தவறல் லவை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna vanishes from the rasa dance, the gopis in their song of longing call him a deceiver who abandons women who came to him, while in his presence they had seen only his beauty and kindness.
hinduism.explanation: The Gopi Gita shows the gopis’ view of Krishna shifting to reproach in his absence.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise sees only faults in her husband’s absence and none in his presence.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.31 (Gopi Gita) (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hymn; a partial match on reproach in absence, though the gopis’ song is mostly praise mixed with complaint.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that our perception of others’ faults is distorted by our own condition.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural observes how the wife’s perception of faults swings with presence and absence; both texts expose the bias in fault-finding.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); only a loose match on biased perception of faults, in a moral rather than romantic context.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns believers against suspicion and imagining the worst of others.
islam.tie_back: In absence the Kural’s wife imagines only faults; the Qur’an names this habit of negative assumption and warns against it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a partial match on suspicion in absence, but a general ethical command rather than about lovers.

judaism.quote_or_event: Joshua ben Perachiah teaches in Pirkei Avot that one should judge every person favourably, giving them the benefit of the doubt.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah urges a charitable reading of others’ actions.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife judges favourably in her husband’s presence and harshly in his absence; the rabbinic maxim asks for the favourable judgment always.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known mishnah; a partial match on how we judge others, offered as an ideal rather than as an observation about love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one’s own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada counsels against dwelling on others’ faults.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows how fault-finding in absence is driven by longing; the Buddhist verse warns against such fault-finding itself.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a loose next-best match on seeing others’ faults, without the Kural’s presence-absence contrast.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that attraction and aversion come from the mind’s attachment, not from the object itself.
jainism.tie_back: The husband is the same person whether present or absent; the Jain verse explains that it is the wife’s love and resentment that change how she sees him.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a fair match on perception shaped by love and hate, framed as delusion to be overcome.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros, the loosener of limbs, a bittersweet creature against whom there is no defence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho’s coinage glukupikron (‘sweet-bitter’) captures love’s double nature.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lover feels both sides in turn: sweet in the beloved’s presence, bitter with fault-finding in absence.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous fragment; a partial match on love’s alternating sweetness and bitterness, without the theme of faults.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza describes a ‘vacillation of mind’ in which the same thing is at once the cause of pleasure and of pain, so that we both love and hate it.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza analyses how one object can arouse contrary emotions depending on how we imagine it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife experiences this vacillation as her husband appears or disappears from view.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Proposition 17 and Scholium (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known proposition; a partial match on contrary emotions toward one person, in an abstract philosophical register.

kurals.tamil:
உய்த்தல் அறிந்து புனல்பாய் பவரேபோல்
பொய்த்தல் அறிந்தென் புலந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Uyththal arindhu punalpaai pavaraepoal
poiththal arindhen pulandhu.
kurals.meaning: Like those who leap into a flood knowing it will sweep them away, what is the use of sulking when I know it will fail?
kurals.elementary: If you know the river is too strong and will carry you off, it is silly to jump in. The wife says staying cross with her husband is like that: she knows her anger will be swept away the moment she sees him, so why even try?
kurals.university: Uyttal means ‘carrying off, sweeping away’ (of a current), and puṉal pāyvar are ‘those who leap into the flood’; poyttal is ‘failing, proving false’, and pulantu ‘having sulked’. The last word eṉ is taken by Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as the interrogative ‘what (use)?’, giving ‘what is gained by sulking, knowing it will fail?’, with Pappaiah specifying that her anger cannot succeed. The Sivayogi Sivakumar gloss on ytamizh instead reads eṉ as ‘I’ (‘knowing it will come to nothing, I sulk’), and Pope’s couplet likewise renders it as a confession (‘So did I anger feign’), so the line can be read as a rhetorical question or as a rueful admission. The flood simile expresses the overwhelming force of the desire for reunion that the chapter describes. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a strong wind sweeps away a boat on the water, even one of the roaming senses on which the mind focuses can carry away a man’s intelligence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a sense on which the mind dwells can sweep away one’s judgment like wind carrying off a boat.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife knows her resolve will be swept away by love as surely as a swimmer by the flood; the Gita uses the same image of being carried off on water.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.67 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a partial match on being swept away on water by the pull of the senses, though the Gita warns against it rather than accepting it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.”
christianity.explanation: The Song declares love stronger than any flood.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural pictures sulking swept away by a flood of love; the Song names love as the force no flood can overcome.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); shares the flood imagery and love’s overwhelming strength, though the roles of flood and love are reversed.

islam.quote_or_event: “And spend in the way of Allah and do not throw [yourselves] with your [own] hands into destruction [by refraining].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids knowingly casting oneself into ruin.
islam.tie_back: The Kural compares futile sulking to knowingly leaping into a flood; the Qur’an names the folly of throwing oneself into destruction, though its context is spending in God’s cause.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a loose next-best match on knowingly courting ruin, in an unrelated context.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water; therefore leave off contention, before the quarrel break out.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares starting a quarrel to releasing water that cannot be controlled, and advises stopping before it begins.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, uses the image of water to argue that sulking is futile and better abandoned.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a good match pairing water imagery with advice to drop a quarrel, though not about lovers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells of a man carried along by a pleasant, alluring river, warned by someone on the bank that downstream lie whirlpools and monsters; the river stands for craving and the pleasant current for the senses.
buddhism.explanation: The Itivuttaka uses the image of a river current to show how desire carries a person off.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s flood that sweeps the swimmer away is the same image of desire’s current, though the Buddhist parable urges escape.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known simile; a good match on being swept off by the current of desire, with the opposite evaluation.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Just as an impassioned buffalo who dives in cold water, is taken hold of by a crocodile and dies.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares one enslaved by the pleasures of touch to a buffalo that plunges into water and is seized.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural, too, pictures plunging into water and being carried off, though for the Jain text the plunge is into ruinous passion.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.76 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; Jacobi gives this line in his summary of verses 74-86)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial match on plunging into water to one’s undoing, as a warning against passion.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Leander swam the Hellespont each night to reach Hero, and on a stormy night plunged in again despite the danger and was drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: The legend of Hero and Leander shows a lover throwing himself into dangerous waters for love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural compares love’s pull to leaping into a flood; Leander literally does so.
greek_mythology.source: Musaeus, Hero and Leander (paraphrase; cf. Ovid, Heroides 18-19)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous legend; a strong image match on plunging into water for love, though Leander is reckless rather than resigned.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza quotes Ovid’s Medea: I see and approve the better, yet I follow the worse, as an example of how knowledge of the good does not by itself restrain a strong emotion.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza explains that true knowledge can be overpowered by emotion, so people act against what they know.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife knows her sulking will fail yet sulks anyway, like the swimmer who knows the flood will take him.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics IV, Proposition 17, Scholium (paraphrase; quoting Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.20-21)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a good match on acting against one’s own knowledge under emotion.

kurals.tamil:
இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும் களித்தார்க்குக்
கள்ளற்றே கள்வநின் மார்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Iliththakka innaa seyinum kaliththaarkkuk
kallatrae kalvanin maarbu.
kurals.meaning: You thief! Though it brings me shameful pain, your embrace is to me what wine is to the drinker who keeps craving more.
kurals.elementary: Some people keep going back to something even when it is bad for them, because they just can’t resist it. The wife playfully calls her husband a ‘thief’ who stole her heart: even when he hurts her by being away, she can’t stop wanting to be close to him.
kurals.university: The wife addresses her husband as kaḷva (‘thief’, a term of endearment for one who has stolen her heart, with a hint of reproach). Iḷittakka iṉṉā ceyiṉum means ‘though it does painful things fit to bring disgrace’; kaḷittārkku kaḷ aṟṟē, ‘like toddy to those who have revelled in it’; niṉ mārpu, ‘your breast’, i.e. his embrace. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss it as toddy that, despite the shame it brings, makes drinkers crave it more and more; Kalaignar renders kaḷva as ‘thief who stole my heart’; Solomon Pappaiah uses ‘deceiver’ and adds that the husband reads her thoughts in her glance and comforts her, a bridge to 1290. The wine comparison returns from 1281 but now stresses compulsive attraction despite harm, recalling the ruinous drinker of chapter 93. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna comes to Radha at dawn bearing the marks of a night spent elsewhere, she rebukes him bitterly as a deceiver, yet her love for him remains undiminished.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s Radha is wounded by Krishna but cannot stop loving him.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise calls her husband a ‘thief’ yet craves his embrace like a drinker his wine.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known canto; a reasonable match on reproach mingled with undying love, without the wine simile.

christianity.quote_or_event: “They have stricken me, shalt thou say, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I felt it not: when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs describes the drunkard who, though harmed by wine, resolves to seek it again as soon as he wakes.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s simile is the same: the drinker returns to wine despite the shame and pain, as the wife to her husband’s embrace.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close match on the drinker’s compulsive return despite harm, though Proverbs offers it as a warning, not a love-image.

islam.quote_or_event: “They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, ‘In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an acknowledges that wine has some appeal but declares its harm the greater.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s comparison rests on wine’s pull despite its harm, which the Qur’an names directly.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a partial match on wine’s harmful attraction, used as legal guidance rather than as a simile for love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend and an adulteress, even as the LORD loveth the children of Israel, though they turn unto other gods, and love cakes of raisins.”
judaism.explanation: Hosea is told to keep loving a wife who has wronged him, as God keeps loving Israel.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife keeps loving a husband who causes her pain; Hosea models love that persists despite injury.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a partial match on love enduring hurt, though Hosea’s situation is prophetic allegory of a far graver betrayal.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares a man given to sensual pleasure to a leper who scratches his sores and cauterises them over a fire, finding relief in the very thing that worsens his wounds.
buddhism.explanation: In the Magandiya Sutta, sensual craving is pictured as finding pleasure in what actually harms.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s drinker who craves wine despite its shame is the same pattern the Buddha describes.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 75, Magandiya Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known simile; a good match on craving what harms, with the Buddhist aim of renouncing it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares one enslaved by attraction to a moth drawn into the flame.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife is drawn to the embrace that pains her as a drinker to wine; the Jain moth image captures the same fatal attraction.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial match on irresistible attraction despite harm, presented as a warning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Helen scorns Paris after his defeat by Menelaus, but when Aphrodite insists, she goes to him nonetheless, unable to resist the goddess of desire.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Iliad, Helen despises Paris’s weakness yet is drawn back to him by Aphrodite’s power.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise reproaches the ‘thief’ yet cannot keep from his embrace.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 3.383-447 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene; a partial match on reproach yielding to attraction, though Helen acts under divine compulsion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato tells of Leontius, who, angry at himself, still ran to gaze at corpses by the city wall, crying to his eyes to take their fill of the sight.
philosophy.explanation: The Republic uses the story to show desire overpowering the part of the soul that disapproves.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, like Leontius, is drawn irresistibly to what she half-reproaches.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic IV, 439e-440a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous anecdote; a partial match on compulsive attraction against one’s judgment, in a non-romantic context.

kurals.tamil:
மலரினும் மெல்லிது காமம் சிலர்அதன்
செவ்வி தலைப்படு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Malarinum mellidhu kaamam silaradhan
sevvi thalaippadu vaar.
kurals.meaning: Love is more delicate than a flower; few are those who grasp its finest moment and true nature.
kurals.elementary: A flower petal is so soft that if you squeeze it, it gets crushed. The poet says love is even softer than that, so you must be gentle and patient with it. Not many people learn how to care for it properly.
kurals.university: Malariṉum melliti kāmam: ‘love (kāmam) is softer/more delicate than a flower’. Puliyur Kesikan specifies the flower as aṉiccam, the proverbially delicate flower that withers even at a breath (cf. kural 90 and 1111). Cevvi means ‘ripeness, right moment, perfection’ and talaippaṭuvār ‘those who attain/grasp’; so few attain love’s cevvi. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘few know this truth and obtain its good fruit’; Solomon Pappaiah stresses having the right place, time and circumstances; Kalaignar ‘few enjoy it with the same delicacy’. The couplet is often quoted independently as the Kural’s most celebrated statement on love, and here it explains why both partners must set aside sulking: a love so delicate is easily bruised. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh joins சிலர்அதன்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kama, the god of love, carries a bow of sugarcane strung with bees and five arrows tipped with flowers; in the Kumarasambhava he aims his flower-arrow at Shiva to awaken love for Parvati.
hinduism.explanation: Indian tradition imagines love’s weapons as flowers, signalling its delicacy and sweetness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural calls love softer than a flower; the image of Kama’s flower-arrows makes the same association.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode and iconography; a partial match on love and flowers, but without the Kural’s point that few grasp love’s delicacy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song compares his beloved to a lily, delicate and rare among thorns.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, joins love with the delicacy of a flower and its rarity among the many.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a partial match on flower imagery and rarity, but the Song compares the beloved, not love itself, to a flower.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that God is gentle and loves gentleness, and grants for gentleness what He does not grant for harshness.
islam.explanation: The hadith praises gentleness (rifq) as a quality God loves and rewards.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says love must be handled with more gentleness than a flower; the hadith sets gentleness as a divine ideal.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith (the sunnah.com page did not load in this session); a partial match on gentleness, without reference to love’s delicacy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem: Why should ye awaken, or stir up love, until it please?”
judaism.explanation: The Song’s refrain warns against rousing love before its proper time.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s cevvi, love’s right moment, is exactly what the Song guards: love is delicate and must not be forced.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a strong match on love’s delicate timing, though the Song does not use a flower image here.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Upon a heap of rubbish in the road-side ditch blooms a lotus, fragrant and pleasing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada uses the rare lotus blooming in a ditch as an image of the few who rise to wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural, too, joins a delicate flower with the rarity of the few who attain its essence, though the Buddhist lotus stands for wisdom, not love.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a loose next-best match on flower and rarity, with a different subject.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra lists among the ten supreme virtues mardava, literally ‘softness’, the humility and gentleness that dissolves pride.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics names softness of heart as one of the ten dharmas practised to stop the influx of karma.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls love softer than a flower; Jainism prizes softness of heart, though as a renunciant virtue rather than a quality of love.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.6 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutra; a loose next-best match resting on the shared idea of softness, in a very different ascetic context.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho compares a maiden to a sweet apple reddening on the topmost bough, which the apple-pickers missed, or rather could not reach.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho’s image presents beauty and love as rare, ripe and out of reach for most.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural, too, speaks of love’s ripeness (cevvi) that only a few manage to attain.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous fragment; a partial match on ripeness and rarity, though Sappho’s image is a fruit, not a flower.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Agathon, in Plato’s Symposium, praises Love as the most tender of the gods, who walks not on the earth but in the softest of places, the hearts and souls of gods and men, and who dwells among flowers.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s Agathon describes Love as supremely soft and delicate, living only where there is gentleness.
philosophy.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that love is softer than a flower.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 195c-196b (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known speech; a close match on love’s tenderness and flower imagery, though Agathon’s speech is later questioned by Socrates.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணின் துனித்தே கலங்கினாள் புல்லுதல்
என்னினும் தான்விதுப் புற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannin thuniththae kalanginaal pulludhal
enninum thaanvidhup putru.
kurals.meaning: She showed her displeasure only with her eyes, then, more eager than I to embrace, she melted into my arms.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever tried to look cross at someone you missed, only to break into a smile and give them a hug first? The husband in this poem says his wife did just that: her eyes looked upset, but she was quicker than him to hug.
kurals.university: Here the husband speaks, recalling a meeting: kaṇṇiṉ tuṉittē, ‘sulking (tuṉi, displeasure) only by/with the eyes’; kalaṅkiṉāḷ, ‘she was stirred, melted’; pullutal eṉṉiṉum tāṉ vituppuṟṟu, ‘she being more eager (vitumpu, the root of the chapter title) than I to embrace’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss that she sulked only as far as a glance, and then, wanting the embrace more eagerly than he did, forgot her displeasure and came into his arms; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read the same. The Sivayogi Sivakumar gloss on ytamizh takes kalaṅkiṉāḷ more literally as her eyes clouding with tears. By ending with the husband’s voice, the chapter confirms that the eagerness for reunion was mutual and that it overcame the convention of ūṭal on both sides. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna reappears to the gopis after vanishing, one clasps his hand, another places his arm on her shoulder, while another, biting her lip with knitted brows, glares at him as if wounded by his absence, before all rejoice in his presence.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata depicts the gopis’ mingled reproach and eager welcome when Krishna returns.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise shows displeasure only with her eyes before rushing into her husband’s embrace.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.32.4-8 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a strong match on reproach shown in the face giving way to eager reunion, in a devotional setting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, the father runs to embrace his returning son before any word of apology.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, outruns her partner in eagerness to embrace, any grievance forgotten.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a partial match on eager embrace at reunion, between father and son rather than spouses.

islam.quote_or_event: In a hadith qudsi, God says that if His servant draws near Him by a hand’s span He draws near by an arm’s length, and if the servant comes walking He comes running.
islam.explanation: The hadith pictures divine love outpacing human approach in eagerness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife is more eager than her husband to embrace; the hadith uses the same image of one party running ahead in love.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith; a partial match on love that runs ahead, in a theological rather than marital context.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Scarce had I passed from them, when I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go.”
judaism.explanation: The bride of the Song, finding her beloved after searching, clings to him.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, seizes the moment of reunion with an eagerness greater than her beloved’s.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a good match on eager embrace at reunion, without the preceding glance of displeasure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Buddha first returned to Kapilavastu, Yasodhara stayed in her chamber, saying that if she had any worth he would come to her himself; when he came, she fell at his feet, clasped his ankles and laid her head upon them.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka introduction tells of Yasodhara’s reserve giving way to an overwhelming welcome.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a show of reserve dissolves into eager reunion, though Yasodhara’s greeting is reverential rather than marital.
buddhism.source: Jataka Nidanakatha (paraphrase; cf. tr. T.W. Rhys Davids)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode in the commentarial tradition; a partial match on reserve giving way to welcome, in a context of renunciation.

jainism.quote_or_event: After Prince Aristanemi (Neminatha) turned back from his wedding to renounce the world, his bride Rajimati, instead of resenting him, chose to follow him by taking vows herself.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana tells how Rajimati’s love for Neminatha led her to follow him into the ascetic life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife overcomes her displeasure in eagerness to join her husband; Rajimati also follows her beloved, though into renunciation rather than embrace.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative; a weak next-best match, since the ‘reunion’ is spiritual and the story turns away from married love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope holds back from Odysseus, testing him coldly, until he describes their bed; then her knees and heart give way, and she runs to him, throws her arms around his neck and kisses him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows Penelope’s reserve dissolving all at once into an eager embrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s scene: displeasure shown first, then an embrace more eager than the husband’s.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 23.205-208 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; a strong match on reserve melting into embrace, though Penelope’s caution is a test, not a sulk.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Terence’s line that the quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love became a classic maxim of European moral writing.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman playwright observes that lovers’ quarrels end by strengthening their love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural ends the chapter the same way: a brief glance of displeasure leads straight to a fuller reunion.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous maxim; a strong match on quarrels renewing love, though Terence is a comic dramatist rather than a philosopher.
